example.code:
flowchart LR
  Client --> API
  API --> Service
  Service --> Database
example.explanation: A compact Mermaid diagram shows major components and the direction of interactions without detailing internal implementation.

useCases.title: Communicate the overall architecture before specifying individual components.
useCases.scenario: Early design review

useCases.title: Break a workload into major components and show how they connect.
useCases.scenario: Workload decomposition

useCases.title: Switch to a data-flow diagram when tracing data movement is the primary objective.
useCases.scenario: Data-centric modeling

interview.question: What is the purpose of a high-level system diagram?
interview.answer: A high-level system diagram gives a broad view of a workload or a major part of it. It identifies the main components, shows how they relate, and represents the general direction of data flow.
interview.followUp: How would you prevent the diagram from becoming too detailed? Keep it focused on major components and their relationships, leaving internal implementation for more detailed diagrams.

interview.question: What information should the diagram contain?
interview.answer: It decomposes the workload into its main components and shows their relationships. It also captures the general flow of data through the system, which helps communicate the overall design before component-level details.
interview.followUp: What additional diagram could clarify movement of data in a data-centric system? A data-flow diagram can model how data moves through the system.

interview.question: What do arrows mean in this diagram?
interview.answer: Arrows show the direction of interactions and dependencies between components. The diagram should therefore make communication paths directional rather than presenting components as an unconnected inventory.
interview.followUp: If the goal shifts to modeling data movement specifically, use a data-flow diagram rather than relying only on the high-level system diagram.

keyPoints: Use this diagram to communicate the overall shape of a complete workload or one significant subsection.
Show the major components, how they relate, and the broad path data takes between them.
Make interactions and dependencies directional with arrows.
gotchas: Do not treat the high-level diagram as a detailed view of every component; it is intended to cover the whole workload or a major subsection.
Use arrows deliberately: they communicate interaction and dependency direction, not merely visual connections.

Working through a design::Identifying bo.summary: Find the resource or boundary that saturates first under representative load, then act on that dimension. Use measurement and targeted limits or capacity changes to keep the system within its SLOs.
Working through a design::Identifying bo.explanation: Identify the resource or architectural boundary that reaches its limit first by measuring utilization, latency, throughput, and saturation under representative load. Then align a limit or scaling action with that dimension—for example, throttle at the relevant boundary, add capacity, or isolate the bottleneck.

example.title: Find the first saturation point
example.code:
# Load-test progressively and inspect the component that saturates first.
for rate in 100 200 400 800; do
  echo "Run at ${rate} requests/second"
  # Replace with your load generator and metrics query.
  sleep 1
done
example.explanation: Increase load in controlled steps, then use latency and utilization metrics to locate the first saturated boundary before choosing a mitigation.

useCases.title: Protect an API during bursts
useCases.scenario: A shared API receives sudden traffic spikes and must keep latency within its SLO.

useCases.title: Contain noisy neighbors
useCases.scenario: One tenant consumes disproportionate capacity in a multi-tenant service.

useCases.title: Protect a constrained partition
useCases.scenario: A downstream partition reaches its throughput limit before the rest of the service.

interview.question: How do you identify the first bottleneck in a distributed system?
interview.answer: Measure performance while increasing load and look for the boundary whose resource or latency reaches its limit first. That boundary is the bottleneck to address, rather than scaling unrelated components.
interview.followUp: How should the mitigation be placed? Set the limit or capacity action on the gateway, service, partition, or dependency that represents the saturating dimension.

interview.question: What signals should a throttling control loop use?
interview.answer: Use low-latency signals from infrastructure utilization, application state, and per-principal counters. These signals let the system detect saturation and apply an appropriate response.
interview.followUp: Why include per-principal signals? They reveal whether one user or tenant is consuming the constrained resource and needs targeted protection.

interview.question: What should you do after finding the bottleneck?
interview.answer: At the saturating boundary, cap consumption and throttle requests after usage exceeds the selected threshold. This keeps the workload within an operating range and helps preserve service-level objectives during high load.
interview.followUp: When might throttling be insufficient? If the bottleneck is persistent, increase or reorganize capacity instead of relying only on admission control.

keyPoints: Track resource consumption continuously and reject or delay excess work once the selected boundary crosses its limit.
A bottleneck response can be scoped to particular users or tenants, preventing a single principal from consuming the whole shared resource.
Define explicit enforcement points such as a gateway, service, partition, or downstream dependency so the response is predictable.
Revisit thresholds when workload behavior changes; static limits can become unsuitable as traffic patterns evolve.
The goal is not merely rejecting traffic; it is maintaining useful system behavior and SLOs during both spikes and prolonged demand.
gotchas: A limit attached to the wrong resource will not protect the actual bottleneck; place enforcement where the first saturation occurs.
Treat throttling as continuous feedback: measure the system, enforce limits, and adapt them as traffic changes.
